title: Three suggestions for SATs reform
author: Daisy Christodoulou
summary: Daisy Christodoulou notes that complaints about a too-hard Sats reading paper in 2023 echo those of 2016, and diagnoses three structural problems that persist. First, a single test must measure a very wide range of attainment, creating a floor-and-ceiling trade-off that worsens as the attainment gap widens, and reading has only three texts so one hard text distorts the whole paper. Second, reading tests are really tests of background knowledge, so a test can work statistically while students find it baffling. Third, threshold scores impose artificial categories on a continuous distribution and distort reporting. Her suggested reforms are a two-test or adaptive structure, a slimmer, more specific national curriculum in the Hirsch tradition, and abolishing labels in favour of scaled scores, while admitting there are only trade-offs.
points: One test for the full attainment range forces a floor-ceiling trade-off, and the reading paper's three-text structure makes one hard text decisive.
Reading assessments are largely background-knowledge tests, so a paper can perform well statistically yet leave pupils lost.
Specifying content domains and slimming the national curriculum, following E.D. Hirsch, could make reading tests fairer and lift scores.
Threshold scores draw lines across a continuous distribution and misrepresent progress, so reporting scaled scores would be less distorting.
The author is candid that every reform has drawbacks and the question is when current problems become pressing enough to change.
quotes: If you create a test that is too hard, then the test does not give you useful information about low-attaining students and can also leave them stressed and unhappy. If you create a test that is too easy, then the test does not give you useful information about high-attaining students and can leave them bored and demotivated.

The maths test has dozens of questions, and you can have a mix of easy and hard questions and ramp up gently across the test. There are a similar number of questions on the reading test, but there are only three reading texts. If just one of them is harder than expected it will therefore have an outsize impact on the entire test. If the text is difficult, then even the easy questions on that text are not actually that easy.

Another issue specific to reading is that all reading tests are essentially tests of background knowledge and vocabulary. If a student takes an unseen reading comprehension test and happens to know a lot about the topic it’s on, they can often end up doing much better than if they sat a test of equivalent difficulty on a topic they knew little about.

One possible solution to this background knowledge issue, which has been repeatedly advocated by E.D. Hirsch, is to specify the broad content areas that the reading test will be drawn from. For example, tell schools that the reading test topic will be taken from the history, science or geography curriculum.

For this reform to work, what would be needed was a national curriculum that was a) slimmer and b) more specific about the detail and order of topics to be taught. This would undoubtedly be controversial, but it might also lead to some of the impressive reading score gains seen in areas that have adopted such an approach.

The problem is that these threshold scores are simply lines drawn on a continuous distribution. Students do not come neatly pre-packaged into two or three categories, and there are not discrete breaks between those categories. When we pretend that students are in neat categories, it leads to distortions
